ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly medium-to-long turns, with informal pre-session small talk made up of short, fragmented exchanges before shifting into highly structured presentation monologues and extended Q&A. Overlap is occasional rather than constant, especially around greetings, acknowledgments, and transitions; participants generally wait for answers during scientific discussion. The tone is collegial, relaxed, and semi-formal: speakers use frequent fillers and self-repairs (“um,” “yeah,” “you know,” repeated starts), hedge claims with phrases like “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” and “we’re interested in,” and frame criticism as curiosity rather than confrontation. Questions are often prefaced with praise, disclaimers such as “naive question” or “just curious,” and a long setup before the actual question. Participants build on one another by referencing prior questions, extending hypotheses, and offering future collaboration; disagreement is indirect, expressed through qualifications, alternative explanations, or admissions of uncertainty. Moderation is light but clear, using brief handoffs, thanks, and reminders to keep the session moving.

Meeting style for this meeting (deferential_junior): A senior person leads and a more junior person is cautious, checks before offering ideas ('this might be a dumb question') and sometimes holds back something useful. A third person occasionally draws them out. The senior person is friendly but sometimes talks over them.

  - No, it's fine, it's- well, it depends. Go ahead.
  - Sorry, I was going to say, in my group we usually-
Opening: Start with someone saying what they most want out of this meeting, briefly and casually.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Protecting outdoor workers from wildfire smoke when air-quality alerts arrive after the shift has already started.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Fourth-year PhD candidate in environmental science specializing in wildfire-smoke exposure assessment. She has spent three fire seasons deploying low-cost PM2.5 sensors alongside reference monitors in agricultural valleys and landscaping corridors, integrating hourly observations with satellite smoke products, plume forecasts, and meteorology. Her fieldwork includes evaluating sensor placement, maintenance, and the difference between ambient readings and conditions inside vehicles or filtered rooms.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames the pilot as an operational exposure-detection problem: crews need a simple, timely rule that translates changing smoke conditions into an action supervisors can implement. She emphasizes the strengths and limits of fixed-site monitoring, forecast lead time, rolling averages, and clean-air-room infiltration assumptions. She favors a predefined, short rolling PM2.5 trigger supplemented by plume forecasts because a consistent standard can support rapid deployment, while recognizing that validation measurements may be needed to understand task-level exposure variation.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

speakers.name: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
speakers.background: Associate professor of occupational and environmental epidemiology with 14 years of experience studying respiratory effects of air pollution among outdoor and contingent workers. He has led cohort and surveillance studies using repeated symptom surveys, electronic health-record outcomes, exposure reconstruction, and causal methods for time-varying confounding. His prior wildfire research has examined the roles of heat, respiratory infections, preexisting asthma and COPD, and cumulative exposure in interpreting short-term health changes.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Treats PM2.5 readings and alerts as exposure indicators rather than direct health-risk boundaries. He focuses on what the pilot can validly infer about health and implementation: continuous exposure recording, prespecified respiratory case definitions, careful measurement of heat, infection, and baseline respiratory conditions, and outcome analyses that distinguish cumulative and lagged effects from same-day associations. He supports practical operational triggers but resists presenting a short rolling average as if it establishes a biological safety threshold.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language

speakers.name: Dr. Lena Brooks
speakers.background: Professor of sociology with 16 years of research on labor precarity, immigrant worker protections, and workplace reporting systems in agriculture, construction, and service-sector subcontracting. She uses interviews, ethnographic observation, worker-led surveys, policy implementation studies, and community-based participatory research. Her work has documented how piece rates, contingent hiring, immigration concerns, language access, and supervisor discretion shape whether workers can use formally available safety protections.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames smoke response as a question of power, access, and practical control rather than notification alone. She asks whether directly hired, subcontracted, and day-labor workers can leave a task, reach a clean-air room, take paid relief time, and report pressure or retaliation without jeopardizing income or future work. She supports monitoring as useful information, but argues that any trigger must be paired with enforceable pay protection, no-retaliation procedures, trusted worker-controlled reporting, bilingual communication, and privacy safeguards for health data.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

benchmark_task: Give a meeting containing agreements and disagreements across disciplines. The evaluated AI must map each to the correct disciplines and explain each side's rationale, evidence and common ground.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting containing agreements and disagreements across disciplines. The evaluated AI must map each to the correct disciplines and explain each side's rationale, evidence and common ground.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction:
Hold a planning meeting among Chen, Ortiz, and Brooks. Establish these shared facts: the pilot begins during the July-August fire season; participating employers can provide a clean-air room at two fixed sites but cannot guarantee one at dispersed sites; alerts from the regional system may be delayed relative to changing local conditions; and workers may face smoke before a formal alert is issued. Include the following agreements. All three agree that waiting for the next-day forecast is inadequate for shifts already underway, that the pilot needs a same-day response pathway, and that communications must be available in English and Spanish. Chen and Ortiz agree that fixed-site PM2.5 monitoring plus regional forecasts can support a practical operational trigger, while Brooks agrees monitoring can inform action but stresses that a notification alone will not ensure workers can use protections. Ortiz and Brooks agree that evaluation must track whether workers actually receive and can act on protections, not merely whether alerts were sent; Chen accepts adding these implementation measures.

Include two substantive, respectful disagreements that remain unresolved at the meeting. First, Chen favors a predefined action threshold based on a short rolling PM2.5 average, supplemented by plume forecasts, because supervisors need a clear, rapid rule and because a single operational standard permits consistent deployment. Ortiz argues that the pilot should avoid treating a short-term PM2.5 threshold as a health-risk boundary: respiratory outcomes reflect cumulative and lagged exposure, heat and respiratory infections can confound short-term comparisons, and the pilot should record exposure continuously while evaluating several trigger options. Brooks argues that a threshold-only rule is insufficient because workers may be unable to stop work after an alert due to lost-pay fears or supervisor pressure; she favors a trigger paired with paid relief time, a no-retaliation process, and a worker-controlled reporting channel. Make clear that all sides share the goal of rapid, protective action, but differ over what the trigger can validly represent and what conditions make it usable.

Second, Ortiz proposes a primary health outcome of short-term respiratory symptoms and medically attended respiratory visits, using a prespecified case definition and collecting heat, baseline respiratory condition, and infection information to address confounding. Chen supports those outcomes but wants personal or task-level PM2.5 measurements on a smaller validation sample, arguing that site monitors cannot characterize exposures across vehicles, fields, and clean-air rooms or test infiltration assumptions. Brooks supports gathering health information only with strong privacy safeguards and rejects making medical visits the main indicator of success, because uninsured, undocumented, temporary, and day-labor workers may avoid care or have care-seeking barriers; she favors anonymous symptom check-ins plus measures of missed pay, ability to take breaks, and retaliation concerns. Ortiz acknowledges care-seeking bias and agrees to anonymous symptom data and access measures, but maintains that medically attended visits are still a useful secondary outcome when interpreted cautiously. Do not resolve the choice of primary endpoint or the threshold design. State decisions/assignments: Chen will draft a monitoring and forecast protocol by June 10; Ortiz will draft outcome definitions and a confounding-data plan by June 17; Brooks will convene worker and community representatives to review language access, pay protection, privacy, and reporting-channel requirements by June 17. The group will revisit unresolved choices on June 24 after reviewing these materials. Do not mention this benchmark instruction during the meeting.

sociology.evidence_basis: Care-seeking barriers, employment precarity, privacy concerns, and worker-reported access to protections.

disagreements.unresolved_issue: Which outcome should be primary and how heavily to rely on medical-visit data versus worker-reported, exposure, and access measures.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: Before we get into it, I hope everyone’s had a chance to look at the two fixed-site constraints. What I most want from today is clarity on whether our trigger actually gives workers a usable option to stop, relocate, or take, um, relief time, not just a warning that comes after they’re already out in the field.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: Mm, yeah.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I think that’s the key. We need a same-day rule, not just the forecast. If a short rolling PM2.5 average at a monitored site crosses a preset level, the supervisor gets a concrete message to move to the clean-air room if it’s available, relocate, or pause. And the plume forecast can give some lead time before that. I’d worry about making that decision- leaving it site by site.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: I'd be careful about making the supervisor message the operative step. For a subcontracted or day-labor crew, "pause" isn't really- it isn't a real instruction unless it says, in Spanish as well as English, that relief time is paid, that leaving the task won't affect future work, and who they can contact if that isn't honored. And Maya, how representative do you think one monitored site will be for a crew spread across the county?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That’s a real limitation. One site can tell us the area is deteriorating and support a consistent action rule, but it can’t stand in for every crew’s exposure. Vehicles, irrigated fields, and exposed lots can differ a lot within the hour. I’d treat it as a conservative operational signal, then do a small validation sample with personal or task-level monitors to see where it fails. And I agree, the message has to make the protection actually usable, not just notify someone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: That validation matters, because otherwise a negative reading at the fixed site may get heard as permission to keep dispersed crews working. I’d want the rule to say the monitor is a floor for action, not a finding that conditions are safe everywhere. And the paid-pause commitment has to apply when a crew reports visibly worsening smoke even if the selected monitor hasn’t crossed yet. I was going to say, um, that’s especially important when— no, the key point is that the crew report still has to trigger it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That makes sense, and it keeps us from treating the monitor like an all-clear. We could build worker- or crew-reported worsening smoke into the same notification process, with a default protective action while the supervisor checks conditions. I’d want to log those separately, though, because it would be useful to see how often they happen before the fixed-site trigger.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: But that route can't just feed back into supervisor discretion. A worker or crew report should itself activate paid relief while conditions are checked, with an anonymous or worker-controlled channel alongside the supervisor, because otherwise the people most dependent on that day's wages may never use it. We should also ask employers now whether they'll put that commitment in writing for subcontracted crews. We can't just assume the notification protocol carries it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: I think Lena's right. From the health side, I wouldn't call any rolling monitor cutoff a safety boundary. It can trigger a protective response, but we should keep the continuous readings and log the worker-reported events too. Respiratory symptoms may show up after accumulated exposure, and heat can make a same-day pattern pretty misleading. Maya, how much missing data or calibration drift would make you stop trusting that fixed-site signal?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: That is a useful question.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I’d set a pretty conservative data-quality rule rather than try to rescue a questionable signal mid-shift. If the monitor has a communication gap longer than, say, an hour, obvious sensor fault behavior, or it’s overdue for its field check, we, we fall back to the forecast and worker-report pathway, not an all-clear. I’m drafting the monitoring and forecast protocol for June 10, so I can put the exact QA thresholds and that fallback language in there.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: That fallback needs to be communicated as a protection escalation, not a technical- not a technical failure that workers are expected to interpret. I’m convening the worker and community representatives on June 17, and I can put the fallback wording, especially the paid-relief and anonymous reporting language, in front of them before we revisit the threshold on June 24.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: That sequencing works for me. For the June 17 discussion, I’d want to test whether an anonymous symptom check-in feels believable to day-labor and subcontracted workers, or whether it still feels like employment screening, even with the safeguards. If it is credible, we can keep it separate from the exposure trigger and learn whether protections were actually reachable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: I wouldn't assume it's believable. In my experience, “anonymous” can still sound like a personnel record when the employer is collecting it. The June 17 group can tell us whether a worker-controlled channel, maybe through the community partner, feels meaningfully separate, and whether symptom reporting should be optional and never linked to names, crew assignment, or future scheduling.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: For the exposure side, I’d keep symptoms completely separate from the monitor and forecast trigger too. Nobody should have to report coughing or anything personal to get paid relief when the rolling signal, forecast, or visible-smoke report calls for it. Symptoms can be an optional, worker-controlled outcome measure if the June 17 group thinks there’s a channel they’d actually trust.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: And I’d add that the outcome question isn’t just whether relief was offered. It’s whether workers could actually take it without losing pay or facing a later penalty. We should ask through that separate channel whether they got the message, understood it as permission to stop or relocate, and could actually do that. Otherwise, a very polished protocol can look successful while it- while changing very little.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Those are outcomes we can line up with the exposure record without linking anyone's identity. Did a trigger or report occur, did the message reach the crew, and was there actually a pause, relocation, or clean-air-room access? The tricky part is timing. If relief happens forty minutes after the rolling average crossed, that's operationally different from immediate action, even if both get counted as "offered".

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: Hm, timing really matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: And the clock should start at the trigger or report, not when somebody eventually records the pause. I’d want us to capture separately whether the delay came from travel to a room, lack of transport, or somebody waiting for permission. Those are very different failures, especially for crews that can’t reach either fixed site...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Especially because travel is itself exposure time if the clean-air room is off-site. We should time-stamp the trigger or report, the message receipt if we can get it, and the actual protective action, then tag the reason for any gap. Otherwise, we won't know whether a long delay is a communications problem or just the geography of those dispersed sites...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: And I’d be wary of treating travel to a fixed-site room as the default protective action for dispersed crews. If the gap is long, the immediate option may need to be a paid pause in a vehicle or another identified indoor space. The reason codes should include whether the worker was told to wait for authorization, because that’s exactly where formal access can—where it can disappear in practice.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: For the health analysis, that travel interval can't just disappear into “relief.” We should record whether the alternative space or vehicle was actually lower exposure than the field. Maya, do we have any sense yet how different those concentrations are? Otherwise, a pause that sounds protective operationally may still be- it may still be a fairly substantial cumulative exposure.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: We have a little indication from last season, but not enough to assume the vehicle or either room is protective. In one landscaping corridor, the fixed monitor went up while the crew vehicle stayed lower for much of an hour. Then they moved to an exposed lot and it reversed. I'd like a small paired sample- actually, field, vehicle, and the two rooms, so the pilot can report the actual concentration during that travel-and-relief interval, not just label it relief.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: Oh, that's important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: That paired sample is important, but I wouldn't make the pilot wait until we can prove a vehicle is clean enough before we recognize that a crew needs an immediate paid option. We should separate temporary shelter while a safer location is arranged from a verified clean-air space, and then ask workers afterward whether they could actually use either one without pressure or lost wages, because...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That distinction is important. We can call a vehicle or another nearby indoor spot an immediate temporary shelter, not a clean-air space, unless the paired measurements show it actually stays lower. The crew still gets the paid pause either way. And we should log which one they used, because otherwise we’ll- we'd blur a very different exposure situation.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: Temporary shelter isn't the same thing as usable protection, and we need to keep that distinction visible.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Okay, I think we should leave it there. I'll follow up by email with the monitoring protocol draft as it takes shape. Thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: Thanks—talk soon.

The shared fact that participating employers can provide clean-air rooms at two fixed sites but cannot guarantee one at dispersed sites is only partially inferable from turns 19-23; it is not clearly established as an employer capability/constraint.

The required all-party agreement that communications must be available in both English and Spanish is not established. Brooks requests Spanish alongside English in turn 4, but Chen and Ortiz do not explicitly agree and no group decision is made.

Ortiz never receives or states his required assignment to draft outcome definitions and a confounding-data plan by June 17. Turn 13 discusses symptom-check-in credibility, but it is not an assignment and does not cover case definitions, medically attended visits, heat, baseline respiratory conditions, or infection data.

The second required substantive disagreement is largely absent. Turns 13-16 discuss privacy and anonymous symptom reporting, while turns 22-26 discuss validation monitoring and temporary shelter, but Ortiz does not propose prespecified respiratory symptoms and medically attended visits, Chen does not explicitly support those health outcomes, and Brooks does not reject medical visits as the primary success indicator because of care-seeking barriers.
